lead: The triple point and critical point are the two endpoints of the liquid-vapour saturation curve on a pressure-temperature diagram. At the triple point, solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. At the critical point, the liquid and vapour phases become identical. These two points bound the range of conditions where ordinary boiling and condensation occur. Engineers use them to decide whether a substance is a liquid, gas or supercritical fluid in power plants, refrigerators and chemical processes.
prereq: You need: phase names and saturation from 5.1, and equilibrium and property diagrams from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Phase boundaries and the triple point

blocks.text: On a pressure-temperature (p-T) diagram, a pure substance shows three phase boundaries. The sublimation curve separates solid and vapour. The melting curve separates solid and liquid. The vaporisation curve separates liquid and vapour. These curves meet at one point: the triple point.

At the triple point, solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. For water, the triple point is at T = 273.16 K (0.01°C) and p = 0.6117 kPa. This pressure is much lower than atmospheric pressure (101.325 kPa). Until 2019 the triple point of water defined the kelvin. The kelvin is now defined through the Boltzmann constant, and the triple point remains a fixed, reproducible reference state at 273.16 K.

Below the triple-point pressure, liquid water cannot exist. If you heat ice at a pressure below 0.6117 kPa, it sublimes: it turns directly into vapour without melting. The sublimation curve lies below the triple point on the p-T diagram. At pressures above the triple point and below the critical pressure, heating ice first melts it to liquid, then boils the liquid to vapour.

The figure plots log<sub>10</sub>(p/kPa) against T for water. The sublimation curve runs from low temperature up to the triple point. The vaporisation curve runs from the triple point to the critical point. The melting curve is nearly vertical and is not shown.

The vaporisation curve ends at the critical point. For water, the critical temperature is T<sub>c</sub> = 647.1 K (373.95°C) and the critical pressure is p<sub>c</sub> = 22.064 MPa. At the critical point, the saturated liquid and saturated vapour states become identical. The latent heat of vaporisation falls to zero.

Above the critical temperature, no amount of pressure can liquefy the substance. It remains a gas or a supercritical fluid. A supercritical fluid has properties between those of a liquid and a gas; it can dissolve materials like a liquid and diffuse like a gas.

On a p-v diagram, the critical point is where the saturated liquid line and saturated vapour line meet. The dome-shaped two-phase region shrinks to a point. The isotherm through the critical point has a horizontal inflection: (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = 0 and (∂²p/∂v²)<sub>T</sub> = 0 at the critical point. This is the critical isotherm. Below T<sub>c</sub>, each isotherm has a flat horizontal segment inside the dome, where liquid and vapour coexist. Above T<sub>c</sub>, the isotherms are smooth curves with no flat part.
Some syllabi call the critical state the critical point. The two terms mean the same state: the highest temperature and pressure at which a liquid and its vapour can coexist.

sections.h3: Reading the diagrams and practical use

blocks.text: Engineers read the p-T diagram to choose the right phase for a process. A steam power plant using a Rankine cycle operates below the critical pressure: water boils in the boiler at a pressure well under 22.064 MPa. A supercritical boiler runs above the critical pressure, so the water turns into steam without a distinct boiling point. The steam is a single dense phase.

The triple point warns you about low-pressure processes. Freeze drying and low-pressure vacuum drying run below 0.6117 kPa, so water sublimes there; ordinary vacuum drying at a few kPa still has liquid water. If you assume the wrong phase, your energy balance will be wrong.

When you read a p-T or p-v diagram, check the pressure scale: 0.6117 kPa is not 0.6117 MPa. That factor of 1000 changes the phase. Also use absolute pressure, not gauge pressure. A gauge pressure of zero means atmospheric pressure, 101.325 kPa, which is far above the triple point.

figure.caption: The sublimation curve meets the vaporisation curve at the triple point (273.16 K, 0.6117 kPa). The vaporisation curve ends at the critical point (647.1 K, 22.064 MPa). Notice that below the triple-point pressure, only solid and vapour exist.

spec.aria: A plot of log pressure against temperature shows the sublimation line meeting the vaporisation line at the triple point and the vaporisation line ending at the critical point.

examples.question: A piston-cylinder contains water at 0.5 kPa and 0°C. The piston moves freely so the pressure stays at 0.5 kPa. (a) Is liquid water stable at this state? (b) What is the minimum pressure required for liquid water to exist at 0°C? (c) Describe what happens when the water is slowly heated at constant pressure to 20°C. Use the triple-point values for water: T<sub>t</sub> = 273.16 K, p<sub>t</sub> = 0.6117 kPa.
steps: The triple point of water is T<sub>t</sub> = 273.16 K and p<sub>t</sub> = 0.6117 kPa. At this point ice, liquid water and water vapour coexist.
The given pressure is p = 0.5 kPa and the given temperature is 0°C = 273.15 K. At 0°C the sublimation pressure (ice-vapour equilibrium) is about 0.6117 kPa, essentially the triple-point pressure.
Compare p with p<sub>t</sub>: 0.5 kPa < 0.6117 kPa. The pressure is 0.6117 − 0.5 = 0.1117 kPa below the triple-point pressure.

(a) At 0°C and 0.5 kPa, liquid water is not stable. The pressure is below the triple-point pressure, so no liquid can exist. Any liquid present would evaporate; ice would sublime. The stable phase is vapour.

(b) The minimum pressure for liquid water at 0°C is about 1 atm (≈101 kPa), the melting pressure at 0°C. The melting curve of water slopes backwards, so at 0°C ice melts only near 101 kPa. At pressures between 0.6117 kPa and about 101 kPa, ice is stable; below 0.6117 kPa, no liquid can exist at all.

(c) On slow heating at constant pressure 0.5 kPa, any ice sublimes directly to vapour. The sublimation temperature at 0.5 kPa is slightly below 0°C. No liquid phase appears. Once all ice has turned to vapour, further heating raises the vapour temperature toward 20°C.
examples.answer: Liquid water is not stable at 0.5 kPa and 0°C because the pressure is 0.1117 kPa below the triple-point pressure of 0.6117 kPa; at 0°C liquid water needs about 1 atm (≈101 kPa). On heating at 0.5 kPa, ice sublimes directly to vapour without melting.
examples.check:
p_triple = 0.6117
p_given = 0.5
margin = p_triple - p_given
print(p_triple)
print(p_given)
print(round(margin, 4))

traps: Reading 0.6117 kPa as 0.6117 MPa. The triple-point pressure of water is about 0.006 atm, not 6 atm. A factor of 1000 puts you above atmospheric pressure and gives a completely different phase.
Using gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure. Gauges read zero at atmospheric pressure (101.325 kPa). The triple point and critical point are absolute pressures.

Thinking that above the critical pressure a gas can be liquefied by pressure alone. Above the critical temperature, no pressure works. Above the critical pressure but below the critical temperature, liquid can exist if you compress enough.
Confusing the critical point with the triple point. The triple point has three phases; the critical point has one phase where liquid and vapour are indistinguishable.

Forgetting that the melting curve is not vertical for all substances. For water, the melting curve slopes backwards (ice is less dense than liquid water), so increasing pressure lowers the melting point slightly. The triple point is the only point where all three curves meet.

quiz.q: Define triple point. State the triple-point temperature and pressure of water.
quiz.a: The triple point is the state where solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. For water: T = 273.16 K, p = 0.6117 kPa.

quiz.q: What is the critical pressure of water in MPa?
Explain why liquid water is not stable at 0.5 kPa and 0°C.
quiz.a: 0.5 kPa is below the triple-point pressure of 0.6117 kPa. At this pressure the stable phases are solid and vapour; liquid water cannot exist.

quiz.q: Why does the latent heat of vaporisation become zero at the critical point?
quiz.a: At the critical point the saturated liquid and saturated vapour states become identical. There is no difference in enthalpy between the two phases, so no latent heat is needed for the phase change.

quiz.q: A sample of water is at 250 K and 0.1 kPa. Which phases can exist? Use the triple-point values.
quiz.a: 250 K is below the triple-point temperature (273.16 K) and 0.1 kPa is below the triple-point pressure (0.6117 kPa). The stable phases are solid (ice) and vapour. Liquid water is not stable.

quiz.q: A pressure vessel contains water at 700 K and 25 MPa. Is it a liquid, gas or supercritical fluid? Explain.
quiz.a: T = 700 K > T<sub>c</sub> = 647.1 K and p = 25 MPa > p<sub>c</sub> = 22.064 MPa. The water is a supercritical fluid. It is above both critical temperature and critical pressure.

quiz.q: On a p-v diagram, describe how the isotherms change as the temperature goes from below T<sub>c</sub> to above T<sub>c</sub>. What happens at the critical isotherm?
quiz.a: Below T<sub>c</sub>, each isotherm has a horizontal flat segment inside the saturation dome, where liquid and vapour coexist. The flat segment shortens as T rises. At T = T<sub>c</sub>, the flat segment shrinks to a single point, the critical point, with a horizontal inflection. Above T<sub>c</sub>, the isotherms are smooth curves with no flat part; liquid and vapour are indistinguishable.

quiz.q: Some syllabi call the critical state the critical point. Are these terms exactly the same? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes. The critical state and the critical point refer to the same state: the highest temperature and pressure at which a liquid and its vapour can coexist. The term 'state' emphasizes the thermodynamic condition; 'point' emphasizes its location on a diagram.

beyond: Not for the exam. Supercritical water is used in supercritical water-cooled reactors and in supercritical fluid chromatography. Carbon dioxide above its critical point (304.1 K, 7.38 MPa) is a common solvent for decaffeinating coffee. Researchers study the critical point of mixtures because it shifts with composition. Search for 'supercritical fluid extraction' and 'critical point of binary mixtures' to go further.
